passage: The washing machines at the laundrette in Leeds hummed while Ada, nine, flipped through a crumpled kids' magazine someone had left on the bench. She found her star sign and read it under her breath: "You are kind, but sometimes shy. You have a secret talent people haven't noticed yet." Ada gasped and tugged her brother's sleeve. "Yosef, listen! That's exactly me. I'm kind to the cat, and I was shy at the party on Saturday." Yosef, thirteen, was reading the next sign down. "Mine says I'm kind but sometimes quiet," he mumbled. Ada wasn't listening. She tore the page out carefully, folded it into her coat pocket and patted it twice.

qa.q: Where were Ada and Yosef when Ada read the horoscope?
qa.a: They were at the laundrette in Leeds, on the bench while the washing machines hummed.

qa.q: What does Ada folding the page into her pocket suggest she feels about the horoscope?
qa.a: She feels it truly describes her and wants to keep it, like proof that someone understood her. She has already matched "kind" to the cat and "shy" to the party. 😊

qa.q: At which moment could Ada have noticed that the words fit almost anyone, and how?
qa.a: When Yosef said his sign also called him kind but sometimes quiet. If she had stopped to compare the two, she might have seen the same lines fit both of them, and most people.

qa.q: How might Yosef see the horoscope differently after reading his own sign?
qa.a: Yosef has just read almost the same words under a different sign, so to him the lines may sound written for everyone rather than a message meant only for his sister.

grounding: A child reads a general horoscope line about being kind and shy and is sure it describes her exactly, missing that it fits others too.

passage: Library period, and Afreen had the new children's magazine before anyone else. She skipped the puzzles and went straight to the last page. "Pisces: You like to help others, but sometimes you keep your feelings inside." Her mouth fell open. That morning she had helped the librarian stack the returned books, and she had not told anyone that her tooth was wobbling. "Jagdish," she whispered across the table, "how do they know?" Jagdish leaned over. "Know what?" "About me! It's like they watched me all week." She copied the line into the back of her rough notebook in her neatest writing and drew a small star beside it. When the bell rang, she read it once more before closing the magazine.

qa.q: Which line did Afreen read under Pisces?
qa.a: "You like to help others, but sometimes you keep your feelings inside."

qa.q: Why does Afreen feel the magazine seems to know her?
qa.a: Afreen feels amazed and excited, because the line matches her own week, helping the librarian and keeping quiet about her wobbly tooth, so it seems written just for her.

qa.q: What question could Afreen ask herself before copying the line as a true description of her?
qa.a: She could ask whether Jagdish or anyone else at the table also helps people and sometimes keeps feelings inside. If the line fits them too, it is not really about her.

qa.q: What is it like for Jagdish to hear "how do they know?" without seeing the page?
qa.a: Jagdish is puzzled and has to ask "Know what?" To Jagdish it is just a magazine page until Afreen's excitement makes it seem special.

grounding: A child in a school library is convinced a vague horoscope line about helping others and hiding feelings describes her exactly.

passage: I'm Binita, and my little brother Divyansh is eight. On Sunday he found the horoscope box in the newspaper's children's corner and read his aloud at breakfast: "You are brave, though sometimes you feel shy with new people." He put his spoon down. "That's me! I'm brave on the big slide, and I was shy with the new tuition teacher." Then he ran to show Papa, holding the page with both hands. While he was gone, I read the other eleven boxes. Most of them said almost the same thing in different words. When he came back, he stuck the cutting on his cupboard door with tape. I'm not sure what he was thinking, but he kept glancing at it all afternoon.

qa.q: Where did Divyansh stick the cutting?
qa.a: He stuck it on his cupboard door with tape.

qa.q: What does Divyansh running to show Papa suggest he feels?
qa.a: He seems thrilled and sure the horoscope is about him, because he links "brave" to the big slide and "shy" to the new tuition teacher.

qa.q: What could Binita do next to help Divyansh notice the pattern without making fun of him?
qa.a: Binita could read a few of the other boxes aloud and ask which one sounds like him. Hearing nearly the same words under other signs might help him see they fit many people.

qa.q: How does Binita see the horoscope differently from Divyansh?
qa.a: Binita has read all twelve boxes and found them nearly the same, so to Binita it is general. To Divyansh it feels like a message written only for him.

grounding: A young boy is certain a newspaper horoscope about being brave but shy describes him exactly, while his sibling sees it fits almost anyone.

passage:
Saturday: at the barber shop in Madurai, Madhav, ten, waited his turn with an old children's magazine. On the back page was his sign: 'You are kind, but sometimes shy. You notice things others miss.' He read it three times. How did they know? He tore the corner off carefully and put it in his pocket.
Monday: at recess he showed it to Shankar. 'This is exactly me. I noticed the new boy had no pencil, remember?' Shankar shrugged. 'Okay.' Madhav smoothed the paper flat on his knee like a certificate.
Wednesday: the class teacher asked for volunteers for the school play. Madhav kept his hand down. At home he told his mother, 'It's not my fault. The magazine says I'm sometimes shy.'

qa.q: Where did Madhav find the horoscope?
qa.a: He found it on the back page of an old children's magazine at the barber shop in Madurai.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when he first read his sign?
qa.a: He felt amazed and understood, wondering how they knew, which is why he tore the corner off to keep it.

qa.q: What could Madhav do the next time he reads a line like that?
qa.a: He could read the other signs too and see if the same words fit Shankar or his mother, before letting it decide whether to join the school play.

qa.q: How might Madhav's mother feel when he blames the magazine for not volunteering?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a little worried that a general magazine line is now stopping him from trying something new.

grounding: A ten-year-old boy is sure a general magazine horoscope describes him exactly and even uses it to explain not volunteering.

passage: Sunaina, you're reading me your horoscope as if it were a letter written only to you. Come, sit with your Nandini Nani. When I was nine, in Shimla, my aunt kept film magazines under her bed. I wasn't supposed to read them, but I found the stars page. Mine said, 'You have a gentle heart, though you are sometimes shy with strangers.' I nearly cried. That was me! I was shy with the milkman! I copied it onto a slip and kept it in my geometry box for two whole years. Every exam, I'd open the box and read it for luck. I never once read the other signs. I didn't think to. Why would I? It was mine. Now, beti, read me what the other eleven say, and let's see how many of them are gentle and shy.

qa.q: Where did Nandini Nani keep the horoscope she copied?
qa.a: She kept it on a slip in her geometry box for two whole years.

qa.q: Why did young Nandini nearly cry when she read the stars page?
qa.a: She felt deeply seen, sure the line about a gentle heart and shyness was written about her alone, even the shyness with the milkman.

qa.q: What does Nani suggest Sunaina do, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Nani asks Sunaina to read the other eleven signs aloud, which will show whether the same kind of words would fit almost anyone.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel after hearing Nani's story?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel a bit caught out but also amused, seeing that Nani once treasured a line just like hers.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being certain at nine that a magazine horoscope described her exactly, never checking whether it fit anyone else.

passage:
Last winter my sister Vinita was reading a magazine on the sofa, and she called out, "Sumit, what's your sign? Leo?" Then she read mine: "You are kind but sometimes shy. You like to help, but new places make you quiet."
I sat up straight. That was me! I am shy at new tuition classes. I do help Mummy with the shopping bags. I told everyone at dinner the magazine knew me.
Then Vinita read hers, Pisces: "You are caring, but sometimes you hold back." Papa said, "That's me too." I didn't want to hear that. Mine was still about me, I thought. I cut it out and kept it in my pencil box for weeks.

qa.q: Where did Sumit keep the horoscope after cutting it out?
qa.a: Sumit kept it in the pencil box for weeks.

qa.q: Why did Sumit not want to hear Papa say "That's me too"?
qa.a: Sumit felt excited and special, sure the horoscope described Sumit exactly, and Papa's comment threatened that happy feeling.

qa.q: What could someone in the family ask Sumit to help notice how the lines work?
qa.a: They could read out a few signs without saying which is which and ask Sumit to guess which one is Leo, showing how most lines fit anyone.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Sumit's excitement?
qa.a: Vinita might find it sweet or funny, since she read a very similar line for Pisces and Papa said it fitted him too.

grounding: A child is sure a general horoscope line about being kind but shy describes them exactly, missing that it fits almost anyone.

passage:
Class 4 library-hour note, Friday. From the class teacher.
Sarita found a children's magazine with a star-sign page and read hers out loud: "You are friendly but a little quiet in new places." She pressed it to her chest and said, "This is exactly me! How did they know?"
Pema, sitting next to her, read a different sign: "You are cheerful, though sometimes you keep your feelings inside." Pema said that was exactly her too. Sarita frowned and said Pema's was wrong and hers was right.
What I did next: I wrote four sign readings on the board with no names and asked who fitted each one. Almost every hand went up for all four. Sarita looked at the board for a long time, then laughed.

qa.q: What did Sarita's star-sign reading say?
qa.a: It said, "You are friendly but a little quiet in new places."

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when she pressed the magazine to her chest?
qa.a: She felt delighted and seen, sure that the reading was written about her in particular.

qa.q: Why was the board activity a useful choice?
qa.a: It let the children see for themselves that almost everyone fitted all four readings, without anyone telling Sarita she was wrong.

qa.q: How might Pema feel when Sarita says Pema's reading is wrong?
qa.a: Pema may feel a bit hurt or confused, since Pema felt the same excitement about her own reading.

grounding: A child is sure a general star-sign line describes her exactly, until a class activity shows it fits almost everyone.

passage:
Sunday, at Nani's house
Nani's newspaper has a horoscope box on the back page. Ayesha and I read them while Nani cooked. Mine said: "You are kind to others but sometimes shy. A small surprise is coming."
It is SO true. I am shy when guests come. And I am kind, I gave Ayesha half my kulfi yesterday. And the surprise: Nani made kheer! The newspaper knew.
Ayesha said hers also said something about being shy. I told her hers is just a copy. Mine is the real one.
I cut it out and stuck it inside this diary. From now on I will read it every Sunday.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Nani make that Dilnaz counted as the surprise?
qa.a: Nani made kheer.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz feel about the horoscope, and what shows it?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels thrilled and understood, writing "SO true" and sticking the cutting in the diary to read every Sunday.

qa.q: What question could Nani ask Dilnaz to help test the horoscope?
qa.a: Nani could ask whether the shy-but-kind line also fits Ayesha and other cousins, or read a different sign aloud to see if it seems just as true.

qa.q: What is it like for Ayesha when Dilnaz calls hers a copy?
qa.a: Ayesha might feel brushed aside, since her reading felt just as personal to her.

grounding: A child treats a general newspaper horoscope line as a perfect description, not noticing it would fit almost anyone.

In the Madrid flat, Mina lay on the rug with the children's magazine her grandmother had brought. On the last page was "Your Stars". Under Pisces it said: "You are kind but sometimes shy. Soon a small wish will come true."
Mina sat up. That was her, exactly. She did hide behind Abuela at parties, and she had given half her sandwich to the new girl on Monday. At dinner she read it aloud. "It knows me! How does it know me?"
Her brother Alejandro opened his mouth, but Abuela patted his hand. Mina cut out the square and stuck it on her mirror, and that night she lay awake wondering which small wish would come true.

qa.q: What did Mina's horoscope say would come true?

qa.q: What was Mina feeling as she lay awake that night?

qa.a: Abuela may want to protect Mina's happy moment and not have her feel silly in front of the family.

grounding: Shows a child certain that a vague magazine horoscope describes her exactly, not noticing it would fit nearly anyone.

passage:
In the school library's magazine corner, Rajni flipped to the horoscope while waiting for the bell. Virgo: "You are kind but sometimes shy. Avoid rushing into new responsibilities this month."
She read it three times. Kind, yes; she'd helped Swati with fractions all week. Shy, definitely. And the class monitor election was on Friday.
"It's telling me not to stand," she whispered.
Swati frowned. "But you'd be a good monitor. You're the one who explains everything."
"The stars know better," Rajni said. At lunch she took her name off the list and folded the page into her diary as proof.

qa.q: When was the class monitor election?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: Why did Rajni read the horoscope three times?
qa.a: She felt amazed and a little anxious; it seemed to know her exactly, and the warning made her nervous about the election.

qa.q: What could Rajni ask herself before taking her name off the list?
qa.a: Whether that line would fit almost anyone, and what she already knows about herself, like being good at explaining.

qa.q: How might Swati feel when Rajni withdraws?
qa.a: Swati may feel disappointed and puzzled, since she believes Rajni would make a good monitor.

grounding: Shows a child who takes a general horoscope as an exact description of herself and lets it guide a choice.

passage:
Losar morning: Dolma found an old magazine at her aunt's house while the family made khapse. Her horoscope said: "You are kind but sometimes shy. You keep your feelings inside." Dolma gasped. That was her exactly!
Two days later: She read it aloud to Anand at the gate. "It's magic. It knows me."
Anand read his own sign. "You are friendly, but sometimes you like to be alone." He stared. "That's me too!"
The next week: Dolma read Anand's line again, slowly. It fit her too. So did her mother's. So did her little brother's.
She frowned at the magazine. "Maybe it fits everybody," she said.

qa.q: What was the family making on Losar morning?
qa.a: They were making khapse.

qa.q: Why did Dolma gasp when she read her horoscope?
qa.a: She felt amazed and excited, sure the line described her exactly.

grounding: Shows a child sure a vague horoscope line describes her exactly, until she notices it fits almost anyone, across a festival week.

passage:
Samir kanna, come, your Paati will tell you something funny. I'm Sangeeta. One hot May holiday, when I was ten, I was staying at my aunt's house in Madurai.
There was a Tamil magazine with a page of stars. Mine said, "You are generous but sometimes stubborn. You worry about others." I read it ten times. I told everyone, "This is me! Exactly me!"
My cousin laughed and read out his line. It said almost the same thing. So did my aunt's. So did the milkman's, when we asked his star.
I was so annoyed. But I also felt a bit silly. I had wanted it to be about only me.

qa.a: The cousin probably felt amused, enjoying showing that the horoscopes were alike.

The train to Kolkata was packed for the Durga Puja holidays, and the fan above their berth didn't work. Leela, sticky and bored, found a magazine under the seat.
She turned to the horoscopes. "You are kind but sometimes shy. You like to help others." She sat up. "Sumit! This is me! It's perfect!"
Her brother grabbed the magazine and read his own. "You are kind but sometimes shy. You like to help others." It was word for word the same, under a different sign.
Leela snatched it back. She checked two more signs. They said nearly the same.
"Oh," she said, and put the magazine back under the seat.

qa.q: Why were the fans a problem on the train?
qa.a: The fan above their berth didn't work.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she said the horoscope was perfect?
qa.a: She felt excited and understood, sure the line described her exactly.

qa.q: What could Leela remember the next time a horoscope feels perfect?
qa.a: That she should check whether it would fit other people too, like Sumit's sign did.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel when he reads the same line?
qa.a: Sumit probably feels amused, seeing that the "perfect" horoscope fits him just as well.

grounding: Shows a child sure a horoscope line fits her exactly, not noticing it would fit almost anyone, until a sibling's line matches.
